introduction: The Public Farm sits on Sunday, and Duchess has the motion in front of her. The Old Pond kept for the Meadow-Born. Everyone who arrived here sent to the road trough instead. Tobias speaks for it, and forty-one animals have already said yes. You are Rue. Six weeks here. Nobody standing behind you. And the only animal in this meadow who has had his arm down that drain.
introductionSummary: The floor decides whether the arrivals lose the pond. Tobias has forty-one names; you have the one thing nobody else went and looked at.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Answering the animal instead of the argument. Tobias never raises his voice. His attacks arrive as sympathy, which is what makes them hard to name out loud.
Treating a crowd as a reason. Forty-one animals agreeing is not forty-one animals checking, and he never once says what any of them looked at.

sentences.text: Duchess. Friends. I did not want to bring this. But the water has gone bad, and somebody had to stand up.
Forty-one animals have put their names to this. Forty-one. That is not a mistake. That is a farm making up its mind.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The count is the whole argument. He never says what a single one of the forty-one went and looked at.

sentences.text: And nobody blames the new ones. Nobody. It is only that Roo here eats out of a bin. He cannot help that. But a bin animal has his own idea of clean.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The question is what is dirtying the pond. He answers it by saying where Rue eats, and dresses it as kindness so it is harder to argue with.

statement.summary: He opens gently. The headcount has already decided, and the one animal who disagrees is ruled out by his supper instead of his evidence.

options.reason: He said something about you and you said something about them. The floor now has two sets of animals and still nothing about the water.
options.summary: You go after the forty-one as a group, and the floor turns into a quarrel about kinds of animal.

sentences.text: Forty-one of them, and not one has done a day's work here. They stand in that water all morning. Then they complain about it.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It answers the motion by describing the animals behind it. Whether they are lazy says nothing about what is coming through the outflow.

options.reason: True, and everyone will feel sorry for you, and nothing moves. You have agreed the pond is his to hand out and asked him to hand it out more kindly.
options.summary: You argue the road trough is unfair, which quietly agrees that the pond is theirs to hand out.

sentences.text: The road trough is half a mile off. It is dry by noon. It tastes of the road. That is not a fair place to send anyone.

options.reason: It puts the real question up before anybody is sent anywhere. Something is dirtying the pond, that something has a cause, and a cause can be gone and looked at.
options.summary: You put cause on the floor. Something is dirtying the water, and a thing with a cause can be gone and looked at tonight.

sentences.text: Something is making that water dirty. That is the question in front of us. Not who drinks there. A thing like that has a cause, and a cause can be gone and looked at. We could look tonight, before anyone walks half a mile.

options.reason: You asked whether they are clever enough to have a view. Even if the answer is no, it is a question about them and not about the drain.
options.summary: You ask whether the forty-one would even know a drain, which is a question about them.

sentences.text: Could any of your forty-one tell a drain from a ditch? Walk them down and find out.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It goes at how clever the animals agreeing are, rather than at what they agreed on.

options.reason: He will answer it honestly and it will cost him nothing. You have agreed that counting is the right tool and only argued about the sum.
options.summary: You query the arithmetic of the count, which keeps counting as the way to settle it.

sentences.text: Is forty-one most of this farm? Or just most of the ones you asked?

options.reason: The one question a headcount cannot survive. It does not say they are wrong to agree. It asks what any of them agreed on.
options.summary: You ask how many of the crowd have actually been to the outflow. The count has no answer to that.

sentences.text: Of your forty-one — how many have walked down to the outflow and looked at the grate?
None of them. None of them ever needed to. Rufus, you have made this a contest about which of us is the better animal. You lost that one before I stood up.

statement.summary: He takes the insult cheerfully and points out that Rue has picked the one contest he cannot win.

sentences.text: Most of the ones who came. That is what most has always meant here. Bring more, if you can find them.

statement.summary: He answers plainly, redefines a majority as whoever turned up, and invites Rue to go and find more.

sentences.text: I do not know. I never asked them. I have stood at that water every morning of my life. I took that for the same thing as looking at it. It is not, is it.

statement.summary: He cannot say, and hears himself admit that standing beside water all his life is not the same as examining it.

sentences.text: Then let me ask you one, Roo.
Forty-one animals have lived by that water their whole lives, and they say it went bad when the new ones came. One animal has been here six weeks and eats out of a bin, and he says it did not.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Half of it is a headcount standing in for a finding. The forty-one are measured by how many they are, not by anything they saw.
The other half is Rue's supper and his six weeks, offered as the reason he counts for less. Both halves ride in one polite sentence.

sentences.text: Who should this farm believe?

opponentPrompt.summary: He folds both tricks into one polite question and asks the floor to pick between a crowd and a bin.

options.reason: You took his question and answered it with a remark about how he has spent his life. That is his own trick handed back, and the floor will notice which of you does it more politely.
options.summary: You answer by describing how comfortable eleven years made him, which is his own trick handed back.

sentences.text: Believe whichever of us has not stood at that water eleven years without once looking down.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It settles the question by describing Tobias's habits instead of saying anything about the pond.

options.reason: A vote does not find out what is in a drain. You have handed the question straight back to the crowd he walked in with.
options.summary: You suggest a vote, which hands the question straight back to the crowd he brought with him.

sentences.text: Neither. Put it to a vote and see where it lands.

options.reason: You pulled his sentence into the two things it was doing, showed that neither is about the water, and named the one that is.
options.summary: You split his question into its two parts, show that neither is about the water, and name the one that is.

sentences.text: That is two questions in one. One is how many agree with you. The other is what I eat. Neither one is what happened to the water. Ask me the third one. Ask me what is in that drain and I will answer it standing here.
Then I will say the hard thing, and I will say it kindly, because somebody has to and I would rather it was me than the yard.

This farm is being asked to drop forty-one lifetimes for one animal who turned up six weeks ago in a mud cart and eats out of a bin. I do not say it to hurt him. I say it because it is the whole of what he is.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Every word of it describes Rue, and it stands in place of a reason to doubt him. The kindness of the delivery is what makes it work.

sentences.text: And I did not decide this on my own. I asked at the trough. Friday night, when the trough is at its friendliest. Forty-one said yes and not one said no. That is not me talking. That is the farm.

logicalFallacies.explanation: He hands the argument to the crowd so he does not have to make one. And he has just told the floor where and when he collected it, which is the whole answer to it.

statement.summary: The set piece. Rue cut down to a cart and a bin, and then the count offered again as though the farm had spoken for itself.

options.reason: He was kind and you were not, which is the swap he would take every time. And it is still an answer about an animal instead of about a pond.
options.summary: You answer his kindness with a remark about eleven years of cart and habit.

sentences.text: You only say that because you have pulled the same cart down the same lane for eleven years. It has left you nothing to think about but who belongs here.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It explains his case away by his life instead of answering it. True or not, it settles nothing about the water.

options.reason: Fixing the detail accepts the frame. The floor is now checking his facts about your arrival instead of yours about the drain, and Cass told you never to defend yourself.
options.summary: You correct the mud cart, which puts your arrival on the floor in place of the pond.

sentences.text: I did not come in a mud cart. I walked. It took four days. I would like that on the record.

options.reason: Cass's phrase, paid off in front of the moderator, with the other side's own animal as the witness. He said what you are; you answered with what happened, and you can show you did not invent it.
options.summary: You answer what you are with what happened, and produce one of his own forty-one as the witness.

sentences.text: locked

unlockedSentences.text: You told this floor what I am. Now I will tell it what happened. The grate on the outflow is bent. The water backs up behind it. The mud sits in the pond instead of going out with the stream. Bram told me that himself, at the fence, before I had asked him anything. Bram is one of your forty-one. That is not a story I brought with me. That is your own witness.

sentences.text: Then let me ask it plainly, Ruin. Rue. Forgive me.
Are forty-one animals wrong and one raccoon right?

logicalFallacies.explanation: It turns the size of the disagreement into the answer. Forty-one against one is a shape, not a finding.

sentences.text: And think for a moment about who has been coaching him. The fox at the west post. The wolf at the fence line. I have nothing against either of them, and neither has anybody else, out loud.

logicalFallacies.explanation: He cannot fault what Rue said, so he prices the animals who taught him. A fox and a wolf, named and then generously excused, which is how the farm has always done it.

opponentPrompt.summary: He shrinks the evening to a shape, a crowd against one raccoon, and then quietly prices the two animals who taught Rue to argue.

options.reason: You said yes and then explained why that lot in particular. The floor heard the second half, and half of the floor is in that lot.
options.summary: You say yes and add that this crowd especially tends to be wrong, which insults the room.

sentences.text: Yes. Forty-one can be wrong, and that lot usually are. Not one of them has ever had an idea on their own.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It answers the question by describing the animals rather than by saying what any of them failed to check.

options.reason: A retreat. He asked whether the crowd could be wrong and you would not say, which the floor will read as no.
options.summary: You back away from the question rather than answer it, and the floor takes that as an answer.

sentences.text: I am not saying anybody is wrong. I am asking about a drain.

options.reason: You take the jab about the fox and the wolf and turn it into what they taught you, then refuse his shape without insulting one animal in it. And the animal who did check was his.
options.summary: You own the coaching, split agreeing from checking, and produce the one member of his crowd who actually looked.

sentences.text: A fox and a wolf taught me. They taught me to ask what happened instead of who is asking. So: nobody here is wrong about what they saw. But agreeing is not checking. And one of your forty-one did check. Hetty chased a moth down that drain and saw the grate bent with her own eyes.

options.reason: You asked about his heart. Neither of you can answer that, and asking it tells the floor you have run out of questions about the pond.
options.summary: You ask whether he would have brought the motion at all if the animal at the drain had been born here.

sentences.text: Would you have brought this at all if the animal down that drain had been born in your meadow?

logicalFallacies.explanation: It puts his motive on the floor in place of his case. Even a damning answer would say nothing about the water.

options.reason: He will grant it at once, because granting it costs him nothing. A bent thing is not yet a cause, and he knows it.
options.summary: You ask him to admit the grate is bent, which he can grant without giving up anything at all.

sentences.text: Will you tell this floor the grate is bent?

options.reason: The way out. He cannot say yes without agreeing the mud has a cause other than you, and he cannot say no without telling the floor this was never about the water.
options.summary: You ask whether the motion drops if the grate is fixed and the water clears, which traps him either way.

sentences.text: If we straighten the grate and the pond runs clear by the frost — does this motion drop?
That is a question about my heart, Roo. I cannot answer it and neither can you. Ask me about the pond and I will try.

statement.summary: He turns it down politely, names exactly what was wrong with it, and asks for a question about the water.

sentences.text: It is bent. It has been bent for years. The pond only went brown this spring. You will need more than a bent thing.

statement.summary: He grants it at once, then points out that something bent for years does not explain a change this spring.

sentences.text: If the pond runs clear, the pond runs clear. A motion about brown water would have nothing left to stand on. I will not say one word more than that.

statement.summary: He gives the smallest possible yes and stops, because the next sentence would hand over the cause outright.

sentences.text: Friends. Eleven years at that water. Same lane, same cart, same hill — my back can tell you all about it. I have never asked this farm for one thing before tonight.
Forty-one of you have already said yes. I would much rather that was the end of it than stand here and say the rest.

logicalFallacies.explanation: He closes on the count and asks the floor to let the count finish the argument for him.

sentences.text: The rest is only this. We are being asked to take our water on the word of an animal who eats out of a bin. I am sorry to put it so plainly. It is still true.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The last thing the floor hears before it decides is what Rue eats, handed over as though it were a fact about the pond.

statement.summary: He closes on the count, says sorry in advance, and leaves the floor holding a fact about Rue's supper instead of one about the water.

options.reason: The last thing this floor will remember is two animals arguing about supper. The pond is exactly as brown as it was when you stood up.
options.summary: You close by turning his supper against him, and the floor goes home having heard a row about food.

sentences.text: And you take yours from a trough nobody has scrubbed since your grandmother pulled that cart. Let us all be very careful about suppers.

logicalFallacies.explanation: It answers a remark about Rue's supper with a remark about Tobias's. Two animals, no pond.

options.reason: You defended yourself, which is the one thing Cass told you never to do. Nobody accused you of dirtying anything. They simply built the evening so that you would want to say this.
options.summary: You close by defending your own character, which is the trap the whole motion was built to spring.

sentences.text: I would like the record to show I have never fouled anything here. Not once. Not in six weeks.

options.reason: You took the insult and made it the reason you are worth hearing, gathered both of his own witnesses, and then made your case something the farm can test. That is the opposite of both of the things he did all evening.
options.summary: You agree about the bins, make that the reason you know, gather both of his witnesses, and offer to lose if the water does not clear.

sentences.text: He is right. I eat out of the bins. Tuesdays are the good day. That is also how I know what is in your water. I have had my arm in that drain up to the shoulder. Only two of your forty-one have been near it — Hetty, going after a moth, and Bram, who told me at the fence. So straighten the grate. If the pond is not clear by the frost, bring the motion back and I will haul the fence posts myself.
So we end as two animals arguing about supper, and the water is as brown as it was when we started. Well fought, Roo.

statement.summary: He notes the evening has finished where he wanted it, with the water untouched, and gets the name wrong once more.

sentences.text: Nobody said you had, Rufus. That is the trouble with it. Nobody ever had to.

statement.summary: He points out, almost gently, that no accusation was ever made, which is exactly why the defence cost so much.

sentences.text: Rue. Your name is Rue. I have had it wrong all evening and I am no longer sure that was an accident. Straighten the grate, then. I will hold the lamp.

statement.summary: He uses the right name for the first time all evening, works out why he had not been, and offers to hold the lamp.
